events/1283_beatrice/phases/0/transition: At the lectern, Boccaccio opens the Vita Nuova.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/0/announceme: Boccaccio: “In his whole life he spoke to her only a few times. She married a banker. He married a wife chosen for politics. Yet in the Divine Comedy the one who leads him up to Heaven is not his wife — it is her. How did that happen?”
events/1283_beatrice/phases/1/narrative: Eighteen years old. The Arno in the morning light. A woman in white comes across the bridge with two companions.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/1/instructio: Click the people at the bridge, and write this moment down.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/1/npcs/0/dia: She crosses the bridge, turns her face toward him, and gives him a small nod.
In that moment I seemed to see the very limit of happiness.
Her greeting had a gentleness in it I have no words for. I was dazed. I ran back to my room like a man escaping a crowd, and began to think about her.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/1/npcs/1/dia: Off in a daze again? Write it down, Durante.
What we write is the “sweet new style” — love is not a knight's prize. It is the thing that makes a soul noble.
When it's written, bring it to me. You call me your first friend — don't hand me some ordinary sonnet.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/1/npcs/2/dia: That is Bice of the Portinari — already promised to one of the Bardi.
Every poet in the city is writing about her. She just goes on greeting everyone kindly, the way she always has.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/2/transition:
June 1289, Campaldino. Dante, twenty-four, rode in the front rank of the light cavalry and fought all day.
Afterwards he almost never spoke of that battle.

The war was over.
But the next summer the funeral bells of Florence
rang for a woman of twenty-four.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/3/title: The City Has Become a Widow
events/1283_beatrice/phases/3/panels/0/d: The bridge is empty. That gentle greeting will never come again.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/3/panels/1/d: A funeral procession in white carries white flowers through the whole city.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/3/panels/2/d: In the Vita Nuova he mourns her with a line out of Lamentations — the way you mourn a holy city that has fallen.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/4/title: The End of the Vita Nuova
events/1283_beatrice/phases/4/narrative: After the grief, the Vita Nuova needs an ending.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/4/question: After the grief, what will you write for her?
events/1283_beatrice/phases/4/options/0/: Write every last lament, then forget her
You won't forget. We both know that.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/4/options/1/: Write nothing more of her — until I can “write of her as no one ever has”

Until I am worthy of her, I put down my pen.
If Heaven grants me the years, I will write of her what has never been written of any woman.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/4/conclusion: The Vita Nuova ends there. He really did stop. The vow waited twenty years — waited until he had lost everything — before it was kept, at a length of more than fourteen thousand lines. And the keeping of it starts with her, waiting for him at the top of the mountain of Purgatory: “Look at me well. I am, I truly am, Beatrice.”
events/1283_beatrice/phases/5/transition: At the lectern, Boccaccio lays the last chapter of the Vita Nuova side by side with Purgatorio XXX.
events/1283_beatrice/phases/5/announceme: Boccaccio: “Gentlemen — she is not his ‘girlfriend.’ She is a god he built for himself. Understand that, and you have found the door of the Comedy.”
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/0/question: Which battle did Dante fight in as a light cavalryman in 1289?
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/0/explanation: In 1289 Florence met Arezzo on the plain of Campaldino. Dante was in it, in the front rank of the light cavalry, and said later that he felt “very great fear, and in the end very great joy.” Montaperti (1260) was before he was born; Lastra (1304) was a crushing defeat for the exiled Whites.
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/1/question: After Beatrice died, what did Dante vow at the end of the Vita Nuova?
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/1/options/0: To write every lament for her, then let her go
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/1/options/1: Never to marry, and to enter a monastery
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/1/options/2: To write nothing more of her, until he could write of her as no one ever has
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/1/options/3: To build a chapel for her
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/1/explanation: The last chapter of the Vita Nuova: Dante puts down his pen until he can “write of her what has never been written of any woman.” Twenty years later the Comedy keeps that vow — she becomes the guide who leads him up to Heaven.
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/2/question:
Purgatorio XXX. She appears at the top of the mountain of Purgatory and says:
“Look at me well. I am, I truly am, ___”
quiz/1283_beatrice/quizzes/2/explanation: Purgatorio XXX: Virgil slips away without a word, and Beatrice arrives — “Guardaci ben! Ben son, ben son Beatrice.” They parted at the bridge; they meet again at the top of the mountain of Purgatory. The vow of the Vita Nuova is kept here.
